questions.question: What does the closure condition require of a vector space?
options: Every vector in the space must have unit norm
The scalar product of any two vectors must be zero
Adding any two vectors, or multiplying any vector by a scalar, gives another vector in the same space
The space must contain no null element

questions.question: In the two-dimensional example, the same vector is written (2, 2) in the Cartesian basis and (2.4, 0.8) in a second basis. What does this show?
options: The vector's magnitude changes when the basis changes
The two bases describe two different vectors
Only the Cartesian basis can describe a vector in a plane
The components of a vector depend on the chosen basis, while the vector itself is unchanged

questions.question: For r₁ = 2i + 4j − 5k and r₂ = i + 2j + 3k, what is the unit vector parallel to r₁ + r₂?
Which of the following is NOT a vector space according to the notes?
options: The set of polynomials of degree n (exactly n)
The space M_mn of all m × n matrices
The space P_n of polynomials of degree at most n
The space of all continuous functions

questions.question: A student says the cross product a × b can be used to multiply vectors in any vector space. Is this correct?
options: No; the cross product can only be defined in three-dimensional vector spaces
Yes; it is defined in every finite-dimensional space
Yes; but only if the vectors are complex
No; it is defined only in two-dimensional spaces

questions.question: Why is the scalar product a · b called basis-independent?
options: It is always equal to zero in every basis
It is always a vector along the first basis vector
It is defined only for the Cartesian basis
It is a single number whose value does not depend on the basis used to express the vectors

questions.question: How is a basis of Rᵐ defined?
options: Any complete set of vectors, whether or not they are independent
A set of vectors that add up to the null vector
A set of linearly independent vectors that also form a complete set (span the space)
Any two non-parallel vectors, in any space

questions.question: For a matrix B, which statement is equivalent to 'the columns of B are linearly independent'?
options: The reduced row echelon form of B has a pivot in every row
The system Bx = 0 has only the trivial solution x = 0
The columns of B are mutually orthogonal
The null space of B has dimension m

questions.question: For v₁ = (1,1,2), v₂ = (1,2,4), v₃ = (3,1,2) and v = (3,2,4), the solutions of Bx = v are x₁ = 4 − 5x₃ and x₂ = −1 + 2x₃. Which coefficients (x₁, x₂, x₃) result from choosing x₃ = 1?
For v₁ = (1,1,2), v₂ = (1,2,3), v₃ = (4,5,9), v₄ = (3,1,2), the row-reduced matrix has no pivot in the third column. What can be concluded?
options: v₄ is a linear combination of v₁, v₂, v₃
v₃ is a linear combination of the others, and v₁, v₂, v₄ are linearly independent
All four vectors are independent because three columns have pivots
Only v₁ and v₂ are independent

questions.question: A student claims f₁ = x² − x, f₂ = x² − 1, f₃ = x + 1 must be linearly dependent because they are three polynomials in P₂. Evaluate this claim.
options: Correct; any three vectors in P₂ must be dependent because P₂ has dimension 2
Correct; f₃ equals f₁ minus f₂
Incorrect; comparing coefficients gives c₁ = c₂ = c₃ = 0, so they are linearly independent
It cannot be decided without knowing the dimension of P₂

questions.question: Express f = 2x² + 4x − 5 as a combination of f₁ = x² − 1, f₂ = x − 1, f₃ = x.
What makes two vectors 'orthonormal'?
options: They are parallel and each is a unit vector
They are perpendicular but may have any length
Their cross product is a unit vector
They are perpendicular (orthogonal) and each is a unit vector

questions.question: What does the condition ⟨ψᵢ|ψⱼ⟩ = δᵢⱼ express for a basis set?
options: All vectors in the set are identical
All inner products are equal to 1
Each vector is normalised (i = j gives 1) and different vectors are orthogonal (i ≠ j gives 0)

questions.question: |Ψ⟩ = (1/√2, 1/√2) and |Φ⟩ = (1/√2, −1/√2). What is true of them?
options: They are orthogonal, since ⟨Φ|Ψ⟩ = 1/2 − 1/2 = 0, and |Ψ⟩ is normalised
They are orthogonal but |Ψ⟩ has norm 2
They are parallel because their components have equal magnitude

questions.question: For |u⟩ = (x, 3x, −2x) with x real, which value of x makes |u⟩ normalised?
Which 2D Hilbert-space vector is a physically valid state without further modification?
A student reports |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² = 1.4 for two normalised states. Evaluate this result.
options: It is fine; probabilities may exceed 1 for complex vectors
It is fine if the states are orthogonal
It is impossible only if ⟨ψ|φ⟩ is real
It is impossible, because 0 ≤ |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² ≤ 1 for normalised states

questions.question: What is a Hilbert space in quantum mechanics?
options: A real vector space with no inner product
A complete complex vector space equipped with an inner product, in which quantum states reside
The set of all real-valued functions of position
A space that contains only orthogonal vectors

questions.question: What is the bra corresponding to |Ψ⟩ = c₁|ψ₁⟩ + c₂|ψ₂⟩?
Why can c|Ψ⟩ (c a non-zero complex number) represent the same physical state as |Ψ⟩?
options: Multiplying by c changes the state but not the energy
Only real values of c are allowed
The overall normalisation of a state vector does not change its information content

questions.question: For the spin state |Ψ⟩ = (3, −2i) in the {|+⟩, |−⟩} basis, what is the bra ⟨Ψ|?
A particle in an infinite well has kets |1⟩, |2⟩, |3⟩, … forming a complete orthonormal set. What is the dimension of its state space?
options: Infinite, because there is a ket |n⟩ for every n = 1, 2, 3, …

questions.question: A student says c₁|ψ₁⟩ + c₂|ψ₂⟩ is not a valid state if c₁ and c₂ are complex. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; coefficients must be real for a valid state
Correct; only |ψ₁⟩ or |ψ₂⟩ alone can be states
Incorrect, but only if c₁ = c₂
Incorrect; any linear combination with complex coefficients is also an allowed state (superposition)

questions.question: How is the inner product ⟨ψ|φ⟩ interpreted in quantum mechanics?
options: As a probability itself, always between 0 and 1
As the energy of the state |φ⟩
As a probability amplitude; its modulus squared gives a probability

questions.question: Why must a physically valid state be normalised so that ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ = 1?
options: So that the state is orthogonal to itself
So that the probabilistic interpretation of the state vector works
So that its energy equals zero
So that its components are all real

questions.question: For |ψ⟩ = (1/√2)(1, −i) and |φ⟩ = (0, 1), what is the probability of finding |φ⟩ in the state |ψ⟩?
For |Ψ⟩ = 2i|a⟩ − 3|b⟩ + i|c⟩ and |Φ⟩ = 3|a⟩ − 2|b⟩ + 4|c⟩ in an orthonormal basis, what is ⟨Φ|Ψ⟩?
Given ⟨Φ|Ψ⟩ = 6 + 10i, a student says ⟨Ψ|Φ⟩ must also equal 6 + 10i. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; the inner product is symmetric
Correct, because both states are normalised

questions.question: What is the squared norm ⟨A|A⟩ of |A⟩ = (2, −7i, 1)?
What is the (i, j) element of the outer product |ψ⟩⟨φ|?
For |ψ⟩ = (2, 3) and |φ⟩ = (1, i), what is |ψ⟩⟨φ|?
What is special about |ψ⟩⟨ψ| for a normalised |ψ⟩?
options: It is a Hermitian projection operator satisfying P² = P
It is a scalar equal to 1
It has rank equal to the dimension of the space

questions.question: Which expression writes a Hermitian operator A in terms of its eigenstates |aᵢ⟩ and eigenvalues aᵢ (spectral decomposition)?
Which is the correct density matrix for the Bell state |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2?
What is the rank of the matrix produced by an outer product |ψ⟩⟨φ| of non-zero vectors?
options: Equal to the dimension of the space

questions.question: If dim V = m and dim W = n, what is dim(V ⊗ W)?
Which set is the standard basis of the two-qubit space C² ⊗ C²?
Using the Kronecker product, what is u ⊗ v for u = (2, 1) and v = (1, 3)?
Given I ⊗ X (X the Pauli-X matrix), what is (I ⊗ X)|00⟩?
Which state cannot be written as a tensor product |v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩ (is entangled)?
A student says a 2-level system combined with a 3-level system has a 5-dimensional state space. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; dimensions add for composite systems
Incorrect; the dimension is the product 2 × 3 = 6

questions.question: Which property defines a linear operator Â?
options: ÂB̂ = B̂Â for all operators B̂

questions.question: Why is the order of operators important in quantum mechanics?
options: Operators can only act on one state at a time
Operators always commute but only in a fixed basis
Operator multiplication is in general non-commutative, so ÂB̂ and B̂Â can differ

questions.question: In an orthonormal basis {|a⟩, |b⟩, |c⟩}, Â|a⟩ = 2|a⟩, Â|b⟩ = 3|a⟩ − i|c⟩, Â|c⟩ = −|b⟩. What is Â as a matrix?
For |Ψ⟩ = 2i|a⟩ − |b⟩ + 4i|c⟩ and Â = |a⟩⟨a| − 2i|b⟩⟨b| + |c⟩⟨c| (orthonormal basis), what is ⟨Â⟩ = ⟨Ψ|Â|Ψ⟩?
Â|ψ⟩ = B̂|ψ⟩ holds for one particular state |ψ⟩. A student concludes Â = B̂. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; one state is enough to prove equality
Incorrect; operators are identical only if they act identically on all state vectors of the space
Incorrect; operators can never be equal

questions.question: What is notable about the unit (identity) operator's matrix form?
options: It is the identity matrix in every basis (Iᵢⱼ = δᵢⱼ)
It changes form whenever the basis changes
It has all matrix elements equal to zero

questions.question: When is the matrix product AB defined, and what is (AB)ᵢⱼ?
options: Only when A and B have identical entries; (AB)ᵢⱼ = AᵢⱼBᵢⱼ
When the rows of A equal the columns of B; (AB)ᵢⱼ = Aᵢⱼ + Bᵢⱼ
When the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B; (AB)ᵢⱼ = Σₖ Aᵢₖ Bₖⱼ

questions.question: What is the adjoint (Hermitian conjugate) of A = [[1, i], [2, 3]]?
For A = [[1, 2], [3, −4]], what are Tr A and det A?
What does det(A) = 0 tell us about a matrix?
options: A is singular, i.e. not invertible

questions.question: In φⱼ = Σᵢ Aⱼᵢψᵢ with Aⱼᵢ ≡ ⟨ϕⱼ|Â|ϕᵢ⟩, what happens if the basis is changed?
options: Both the equation and the matrix elements stay the same
The operator changes into a different operator
The operator equation is unchanged but the numerical matrix elements Aⱼᵢ change

questions.question: A = [[1, 0, −3i], [3, 5, 0], [3i, 0, −2]] has real diagonal entries. A student calls it Hermitian. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; real diagonal entries are sufficient
Incorrect; A₂₁ = 3 but A₁₂* = 0, so Aᵢⱼ ≠ Aⱼᵢ* and A is not Hermitian
Correct; A₁₃ = −3i and A₃₁ = 3i are conjugates, so all entries match
Incorrect; a Hermitian matrix must be symmetric with real entries

questions.question: What condition defines a Hermitian operator, and what is its matrix form?
Why are observables represented by Hermitian operators?
options: They are always equal to the identity
Their eigenvalues are real, matching the real results of measurements

questions.question: Which is NOT a property of Hermitian operators?
options: Eigenfunctions of distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal
Their eigenvalues are always purely imaginary
Their eigenfunctions form a complete set

questions.question: The 1D harmonic oscillator Hamiltonian is Ĥ = p̂²/2m + ½mω²x̂². Why is Ĥ Hermitian?
options: Because it contains a factor of ½
Because x̂ and p̂ are Hermitian

questions.question: How is the Hadamard gate H = (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, −1]] best classified?
options: Both Hermitian (H† = H) and unitary (H†H = I)

questions.question: A student claims eigenfunctions of a Hermitian operator with different eigenvalues need not be orthogonal. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; orthogonality holds only for degenerate eigenvalues
Correct; orthogonality holds only for real operators

questions.question: What is the defining condition of a unitary operator?
options: Û†Û = I, so the adjoint equals the inverse (Û† = Û⁻¹)

questions.question: What does unitary evolution do to the total probability of a state, and where do its eigenvalues lie?
options: It halves the probability; eigenvalues are real
It preserves probability; eigenvalues are real and positive
It preserves total probability; eigenvalues have the form e^{iθ}, lying on the unit circle
It changes the probability; eigenvalues are zero

questions.question: Which two conditions define a projection operator P?
For projectors Pᵢ = |i⟩⟨i| onto an orthonormal basis, which relations hold?
options: PᵢPⱼ = Pᵢ for i ≠ j, and ΣPᵢ = 0
PᵢPⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j, and ΣPᵢ = I (closure)
PᵢPⱼ = I for i ≠ j, and ΣPᵢ = I
PᵢPⱼ = 0 for all i, j, and ΣPᵢ = 0

questions.question: A student says measurement, like every quantum gate, is represented by a unitary matrix. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; measurement is the most important unitary operation
Correct; measurement is unitary because it preserves probability
Incorrect; all qubit operations except measurement are unitary
Incorrect; gates are non-unitary and measurement is unitary

questions.question: How are the eigenvalues of a matrix A obtained?
options: By taking the trace of A
By solving the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0

questions.question: For A = [[1, 2], [3, −4]], the characteristic equation is λ² + 3λ − 10 = 0. What are the eigenvalues?
For A = [[2, 2], [1, 3]] the eigenvalues are 4 and 1. Which is an eigenvector for λ = 1?
For A = [[1, 2], [−1, 4]] (eigenvalues 3 and 2), which eigenvector corresponds to λ = 2?
For A = [[2, −3, 0], [2, −5, 0], [0, 0, 3]], which is the set of eigenvalues?
For [[2, 0, 0], [0, 3, 4], [0, 4, 9]], a student reads off eigenvalues 2, 3, 9 (the diagonal). Evaluate this.
options: Correct; the eigenvalues are always the diagonal entries
Incorrect; the matrix is not diagonal, and its eigenvalues are 1, 2 and 11

questions.question: Which matrix is σ_y?
Which set lists the key properties of the Pauli matrices?
options: Hermitian, unitary, traceless, and each squares to the identity
Anti-Hermitian, non-unitary, trace 1, squares to zero

questions.question: Using the Pauli product relations, what is σ_zσ_x?
What follows from [σ_x, σ_y] = 2iσ_z ≠ 0?
options: Spin components can always be measured together
σ_x and σ_y have identical eigenvalues
Spin components along different axes cannot be measured simultaneously with arbitrary precision

questions.question: Given {σᵢ, σⱼ} = 2δᵢⱼ I, what is {σ_x, σ_y}?
A student says σ_y cannot be Hermitian because it has imaginary entries. Evaluate this.
options: Correct; Hermitian matrices must be real
Incorrect; σ_y† = σ_y, since the conjugate transpose restores the original matrix
Incorrect; σ_y is Hermitian only in the z-basis

questions.question: How is the commutator of Â and B̂ defined?
What is the canonical commutation relation between x̂ and p̂ₓ?
Which product-rule identity holds for commutators?
For H = p²/2μ + ½μω²x², what is xH − Hx = [x, H]?
From [x̂ᵢ, p̂ⱼ] = iħδᵢⱼ, which commutator vanishes?
A student says two observables whose operators have a non-zero commutator can be measured simultaneously with arbitrary precision. Evaluate this.
options: Incorrect; non-commuting observables are subject to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle
Correct; only commuting operators are limited by uncertainty
Correct; commutators only affect the energy
Incorrect; non-commuting observables can never be measured at all

questions.question: In quantum mechanics, physical observables are represented by which mathematical objects?
options: Hermitian operators acting on states in a Hilbert space
Fixed numbers fixed by the exact classical state

questions.question: Which set lists physical properties treated as observables in the notes?
options: Position, momentum, energy and angular momentum

questions.question: How does the quantum description of an observable differ from the classical one?
options: The observable always has one exact value fixed before measurement
The observable has no possible values at all
The observable is replaced by the wavefunction's phase
An operator acts on the state, and a measurement returns one of a set of allowed values with probabilities

questions.question: Which observable–operator pairing appears in the notes' correspondence table?
options: Total energy ↔ Ĥ; position ↔ x̂; momentum ↔ P̂
Total energy ↔ P̂; momentum ↔ Ĥ; position ↔ x̂
Total energy ↔ x̂; position ↔ Ĥ; momentum ↔ P̂
Total energy ↔ P̂; position ↔ P̂; momentum ↔ Ĥ

questions.question: A student argues observables could be represented by any operator. Why is that unsatisfactory?
options: Only Hermitian operators have no eigenvalues
Measured values must be real, so the operator must have real eigenvalues, which Hermitian operators guarantee
Non-Hermitian operators cannot act on wavefunctions
Observables must always have imaginary values

questions.question: What is the position-space form of the momentum operator p̂?
What does the eigenvalue form P̂ψ(x) = p ψ(x) tell us about p?
options: p is always the expectation of x
p is the numerical momentum value measured in the lab if the system is in the state ψ(x)
p is the normalisation constant of ψ

questions.question: What is the one-dimensional kinetic-energy operator T̂?
What is the time-independent Hamiltonian operator in one dimension?
Which observable–operator pairing is given in the notes' table?
In three dimensions, how does the kinetic-energy operator generalise?
What does the eigenvalue equation Ĝψₙ = Gₙψₙ state?
options: The operator is the inverse of ψₙ
Acting with the operator on ψₙ returns the same function times a constant Gₙ

questions.question: For ψ = e^{2x} and Ĝ = d²/dx², what is the eigenvalue?
What does the postulate that only eigenvalues Gₙ are ever observed imply?
options: Every observable can take any real value
Values of dynamical variables are quantised
All observables have the same eigenvalue

questions.question: What is a 'definite state' of an observable?
options: A superposition of all eigenstates with equal weights
A state whose wavefunction is not normalised
An eigenstate in which the observable has a 100% certain value

questions.question: According to the notes' framework, how do you find the possible measured values of an observable and the state for each value?
options: Find the eigenvectors for the values, and the trace for the states
Take the expectation value for both
Find the eigenvalues for the values, and the eigenvectors for the corresponding states

questions.question: A student says the eigenvalue of d²/dx² acting on e^{2x} is 2. Evaluate this.
options: Incorrect; d²/dx² e^{2x} = 4e^{2x}, so the eigenvalue is 4
Correct; the eigenvalue is the exponent
Correct; second derivatives halve the exponent

questions.question: For a normalised wavefunction Ψ, how is ⟨x⟩ defined?
What does an expectation value represent experimentally?
options: The single value obtained in every measurement
The average of the results of many identical measurements
The value of the quantity at a single point

questions.question: For a free particle ψ(x) = Ae^{ipx/ħ}, what is ⟨p⟩?
For ψ(x) = √(2/L) sin(πx/L) in 0 < x < L, what is ⟨p⟩?
Why is ⟨p⟩ = 0 for any real wavefunction?
options: Because real functions have no derivative
Because ψ² is always a constant
The integral reduces to (ħ/2i)ψ² evaluated at ±∞, which vanishes

questions.question: For the harmonic oscillator ground state, ⟨x²⟩ = 1/2A and ⟨p²⟩ = ħ²A/2 with ⟨x⟩ = ⟨p⟩ = 0. What is ΔxΔp?
Using ψ = ax on 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, a student finds ⟨x⟩ = a²/4 without normalising. Evaluate this.
options: It is correct for any value of a
It is only valid after normalising; requiring a²/3 = 1 gives a² = 3, so ⟨x⟩ = 3/4

questions.question: Integration by parts gives which form for ⟨p²⟩?
What did Stern and Gerlach observe in 1922 when a silver-atom beam passed through an inhomogeneous magnetic field?
options: The beam split into two distinct beams

questions.question: Why does the two-beam result contradict the classical expectation?
options: Classically the atoms would not be deflected at all
Classically exactly two values are expected
Classically the spin has no component along z
Classically the spin component would range continuously from −|S| to +|S|, giving a continuous spread

questions.question: What gives a silver atom its net magnetic moment in this analysis?
options: The lone 5s electron outside closed shells (47 electrons in total)

questions.question: What values of S_z did the deflections correspond to, and what is ħ?
The deflecting force is F_z ∝ S_z ∂B_z/∂z. What does the deflection therefore measure?
options: The spin component perpendicular to the gradient
The component of the spin along the z-axis, the direction of the field gradient

questions.question: What do the kets |+⟩ and |−⟩ represent for a z-oriented analyzer?
options: States of atoms leaving the upper port (S_z = +ħ/2) and lower port (S_z = −ħ/2)

questions.question: Is the z-axis special for the experiment's results?
options: No; nothing is special about the z-axis, and any axis gives the same behaviour
Yes; only the z-axis gives two beams
Yes; other axes give continuous beams
No; any axis gives three beams

questions.question: In Experiment 1, two analyzers measure S_z in succession. What is seen at the second analyzer?
options: Half the atoms exit each port
No atoms ever exit its lower port; all atoms from the first analyzer's upper port exit its upper port
All atoms exit the lower port
The atoms are randomly distributed among three ports

questions.question: What role does the first analyzer play in Experiment 1?
options: It changes the magnitude of the spin
It prepares the state (a state-preparation device) for the second analyzer

questions.question: In Experiment 2 (z then x), 50 atoms enter the x-analyzer. How many exit each port on average?
options: 50 from the upper port and 0 from the lower
0 from the upper port and 50 from the lower

questions.question: Would Experiment 2's results change if the lower port of the first analyzer were used instead?
options: Yes; all atoms would exit the upper port
No; the results would be unchanged, with 50% in each port

questions.question: What can be said about which port a given atom exits in Experiment 2?
options: Only probabilities can be given: a 50% chance for each port, with random arrival sequences
The exit port can be predicted exactly
The exit port depends on the atom's mass
Every atom exits the lower port

questions.question: A hidden-variable proposal says each atom carries a pre-determined set of instructions to explain the randomness. What does the text report?
options: Bell proved local hidden-variable theories are fully correct
Stern and Gerlach proved hidden variables in 1922
John Bell proved that local hidden-variable theories are not consistent with quantum mechanics
Hidden variables were shown to explain all experiments without probability

questions.question: In Experiment 3, what is the sequence of analyzers?
With 500 atoms entering, 250 pass the X analyzer's selected port. How many exit the upper port of the final Z analyzer?
What would classical reasoning predict for the third measurement, and what is found?
options: Classically S_z = +ħ/2 (all up); quantum mechanics gives 50% in each port

questions.question: What does Experiment 3 show about S_x and S_z?
options: They are always measured together exactly
They are incompatible observables, so their values cannot be known simultaneously

questions.question: What key feature of quantum mechanics is demonstrated by the 'forgotten' first result?
What fraction of the original 500 atoms exit the final analyzer's upper port?
How does Experiment 4b differ from 4a?
options: The lower beam is blocked and the third analyzer is removed
The upper beam of the second analyzer is blocked and only the lower beam goes to the third
The analyzers are rotated to the y-axis

questions.question: In Experiment 4a, 100 atoms enter. How many exit each port of the third analyzer?
options: 25 from the upper port and 25 from the lower port

questions.question: In Experiment 4c, what does classical probability predict at the third analyzer, and what does quantum mechanics give?
options: Classical: 50% per port; quantum: all atoms exit the upper port and none the lower
Classical: all in the upper port; quantum: 50% each

questions.question: What is odd about the lower port of the third analyzer in 4c compared with 4a/4b?
options: More atoms emerge there than in 4a
No atoms emerge there, although 25% did when only one path was open
It becomes the only open port

questions.question: Which explanation does the text give via the double-slit analogy?
options: Amplitudes are added first and then squared, allowing interference
The atoms are absorbed by the second analyzer

questions.question: To make every atom exit the upper port of the third analyzer, which modification of Experiment 3 would work?
options: Recombine both beams from the second analyzer properly (Experiment 4c)
Block the upper beam of the second analyzer
Rotate the third analyzer to the x-axis
Add a fourth analyzer along the y-axis

questions.question: What name is given to pairs like S_x and S_z whose values cannot be known simultaneously?
What happens in the Erwin's-socks analogy after sorting by colour, then by length, then by colour again?
options: The colour measured first has become random, as if the socks forgot the first measurement

questions.question: Are all pairs of quantum-mechanical observables incompatible?
options: No; some experiments can be done without disturbing certain other observables

questions.question: Why must the recombination of the two beams in Experiment 4c be done 'properly'?
options: To convert spin-up atoms into spin-down atoms

questions.question: Can a cleverer experiment avoid disturbing the system when measuring S_x after S_z?
options: Yes; a better analyzer removes it
Yes; a colder beam removes it
No; the incompatibility between S_x and S_z is fundamental

questions.question: What is the potential energy V(x) for a particle in a 1D box of width L?
options: V = 0 for 0 < x < L and V = ∞ outside the box

questions.question: How does the quantum picture differ from the classical picture of a particle in a box?
options: Classically the particle can be anywhere; quantum mechanically it is described by a wavefunction with some regions more probable than others
Quantum: the particle sits at rest at one point

questions.question: What is the particle's potential energy inside the box?
Why is V = 0 a convenient choice inside the box?
options: Because the walls exert a force inside
Because the particle has no mass
No force acts inside (F = −dV/dx = 0), so the potential is constant and can be set to zero

questions.question: A student says the 1D box is an exact model of a real atom's potential. Evaluate this.
options: Incorrect; it is an idealised model that approximates some situations such as an electron confined in a wire or metal piece
Correct; real atoms have flat infinite walls
Correct; it is exact for hydrogen

questions.question: What general solution applies inside the box?
options: ψ(x) = A sin kx + B cos kx, with k² = 2mE/ħ²

questions.question: Why must ψ vanish at the walls?
options: The wave equation cannot be solved there
The energy is zero at the walls
The potential is infinite outside, so the particle cannot be found there and ψ must be zero at x = 0 and x = L
The wavefunction is always 1 at the walls

questions.question: What does ψ(0) = 0 imply for the constants?
options: B = 0, leaving ψ = A sin kx

questions.question: What does ψ(L) = 0 imply?
